content:
I recently noticed that Apple seems to have abandoned Cinematic Mode, and a video experiment perfectly illustrates my frustration with this fact.

It's not that the feature itself is bad, but rather that it's so close to being usable enough for actual shooting that it's even harder to understand why Apple hasn't properly leveraged the massive leap in computing power from the iPhone 13 (the model where this feature first launched) to the latest iPhone. Let me show you...

I've previously mentioned that I understand why Apple hasn't made updating this feature a priority, but I also maintain that they should, so as to encourage future video creators and filmmakers, especially some young people who might not have any other camera equipment.

I have a friend who enjoys using a smartphone to interview strangers on the street, and she always finds a way to get them to open up and share stories you could never imagine. I decided to reverse the situation, arranging for her to sit on a stool, and likewise use a smartphone to film—this time I used the iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to test Cinematic Mode's ability to handle a relatively simple challenge: a person in the foreground, with a railing about 25 feet behind them, and further beyond across the Thames, the O2 Arena on the opposite bank is nearly a thousand feet away. Additionally, she would be sitting on a stool, so her range of movement is quite limited.

The answer is...almost there. The overall impression is good, but there's a visible halo between CK's feet and the railing, the support pillars of the O2 sometimes come into focus unexpectedly when she moves her head, and the river surface occasionally comes into focus when she spreads her arms:

To be fair, CK countered that the average viewer wouldn't notice these issues when watching the video. If they're not filmmakers or tech enthusiasts familiar with how this feature works, they might not even notice the problems at all, and even if they did, they wouldn't find them bothersome. I reckon she makes a very good point.

But these issues really bother me, and I believe even amateur-level video enthusiasts would feel the same disappointment as I do—and these people are precisely the target audience for this feature.

As I said at the beginning, my frustration isn't because the feature is poor, but because I truly believe that if Apple properly leverages the computing power and neural network processing capabilities of the current generation of iPhone chips, this feature could be significantly improved. In fact, I expect a truly updated Cinematic Mode should be capable of handling even more complex shooting environments than this.

Do you agree with my view? Do you want Apple to give Cinematic Mode a little more love? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
